plans.name: Nutrition for Anaemia (Iron Deficiency)
plans.intro: Anaemia affects over 40% of women and 50% of children under 5 in Uganda. Most cases are iron-deficiency anaemia, caused by insufficient iron intake, poor absorption, or blood loss (including heavy periods and malaria). Diet and supplementation together are the solution.
plans.goal: Increase iron intake and absorption to rebuild blood

eat_more.reason: Richest iron source available in Uganda — one portion twice weekly is highly effective
Most affordable everyday iron source — must pair with Vitamin C food
Very high iron and Vitamin C together — rare combination
eat_more.portion: 2 tablespoons dried powder or 1 cup fresh leaves daily

eat_more.reason: Small whole fish — high iron, calcium, and Vitamin B12. Very affordable.
Good plant iron source — always eat with Vitamin C

eat_more.food: Vitamin C foods with every iron-rich meal
eat_more.reason: Doubles iron absorption — ESSENTIAL with plant iron sources
eat_more.portion: Squeeze of lemon/lime, or half a guava, or tomato

eat_more.reason: Good plant iron, protein, and healthy fats
Highly concentrated iron source
Iron and Vitamin B12

eat_less.reason: Tannins in tea and coffee block up to 60% of iron absorption — drink 1 hour before or 2 hours after iron-rich meals
Calcium competes with iron absorption at the same meal
Reduce stomach acid needed for iron absorption

plans.supplements: Iron tablets (ferrous sulphate or ferrous fumarate) are available at health centres. Take with a glass of orange juice or with a vitamin C food. Black stools are normal and harmless.
warning_signs: Extreme fatigue making it hard to do daily tasks
Yellow or pale yellow skin (consider other causes of anaemia)
plans.uganda_note: Malaria destroys red blood cells and worsens anaemia significantly. Prevent malaria with insecticide-treated nets. Intestinal worms also cause anaemia — deworm regularly with mebendazole every 6 months.

plans.name: Nutrition for Type 2 Diabetes
plans.intro: Type 2 diabetes is rapidly increasing in Uganda, especially in urban areas. Diet is the most powerful tool for managing blood sugar — many people can significantly reduce or even eliminate medication with the right eating pattern.
plans.goal: Keep blood sugar stable throughout the day — no spikes, no crashes
targets: Overweight individuals with family history of diabetes

eat_more.reason: Slower sugar release than refined white posho. Millet posho is even better.
eat_more.portion: Small portion (size of your fist) per meal

eat_more.reason: Low glycaemic index — steadiest blood sugar of all Uganda staples. Best choice.
Low GI staple — good alternative to white posho
Ripe matoke raises sugar quickly. Unripe / green matoke is much better for diabetics.
Very low GI. Protein and fibre slow sugar absorption. Best staple for diabetics.
eat_more.portion: At least 1 cup cooked at every meal

eat_more.reason: Low calories, low sugar — eat as much as you want
Protein without raising blood sugar. Tilapia and Nile perch — excellent.
Healthy fat that does not raise blood sugar. Helps insulin sensitivity.

eat_less.reason: Very high GI — rapid blood sugar spike. Use millet or whole grain instead.
Rapidly raise blood sugar — eat small amounts occasionally at most
Starch has converted to sugar — raises blood sugar rapidly
High GI — if you eat rice, pair with large amount of beans and vegetables to slow absorption

eat_less.food: Sugary drinks — Fanta, Pepsi, Mirinda, sodas, concentrated juices
eat_less.reason: Most dangerous for diabetics — drink only water, black tea, or black coffee
Very high GI — one of the worst foods for blood sugar management
High fat worsens insulin resistance over time
Reduces to 1/2 teaspoon maximum or use no sugar

plans.meal_pattern: 3 small to moderate meals per day at regular times. Never skip meals (especially if on medication). Eat similar amounts at each meal — consistency helps stabilise blood sugar. Walk for 30 minutes after meals — significantly reduces post-meal blood sugar spike.
plans.supplements: No specific supplements. Metformin (if prescribed) causes Vitamin B12 deficiency — supplement B12 or eat liver and eggs regularly.
plans.uganda_note: Diabetes is increasing rapidly in Ugandan cities (Kampala, Jinja, Mbarara). Key drivers: reduced physical activity, increased consumption of refined starchy foods, sodas, and processed foods. Rural Ugandans eating traditional foods of millet, sorghum, beans, and fish have far lower diabetes rates.

plans.name: Nutrition for High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)
plans.intro: High blood pressure (hypertension) affects approximately 30% of Ugandan adults. Diet changes can reduce blood pressure significantly — sometimes as much as medication. The DASH eating pattern is the most evidence-based dietary approach.
plans.goal: Lower blood pressure through diet — reduce sodium, increase potassium and magnesium
targets: Family history of stroke or heart attack

eat_more.reason: Potassium counteracts sodium and directly lowers blood pressure
Potassium, magnesium, protein, fibre — all beneficial for blood pressure
Potassium and magnesium
Calcium and potassium without high sodium if unsalted
Compounds in garlic have modest blood pressure lowering effects
Clinical evidence shows hibiscus tea lowers blood pressure
Magnesium content helps blood vessel relaxation

eat_less.reason: Most important dietary change for hypertension. Target: less than 5g salt per day (1 teaspoon total)
tips: Do not add salt at table
Dried salted fish (mukene, smoked fish) are very high in salt — rinse before cooking
Cube Royco and Maggi stock cubes are extremely high in salt — use minimally or not at all

eat_less.reason: Directly raises blood pressure. Limit to maximum 1-2 drinks/day — ideally none.
Saturated fat contributes to artery damage and hypertension over time
Weight gain raises blood pressure — healthy weight management is essential
Drive weight gain and worsen metabolic syndrome

plans.lifestyle_note: Salt is the most important dietary change. Reducing to 5g per day can lower blood pressure by 5-7 mmHg — as much as one blood pressure tablet. Exercise is also extremely powerful: 30 minutes of walking 5 days/week reduces blood pressure significantly.
plans.uganda_note: Traditional Ugandan salt use is changing — Maggi and Royco bouillon cubes are now extremely common and are very high in sodium. Processed and packaged foods are increasingly consumed. The traditional diet of millet, beans, groundnuts, and vegetables is naturally low in sodium and protective.

plans.name: Nutrition During and After Malaria
plans.intro: Malaria causes fever, anaemia, liver strain, and often loss of appetite. Good nutrition supports faster recovery, prevents complications like anaemia, and strengthens the immune system for ongoing protection.
plans.goal: Rebuild blood, support liver, restore energy and immune function

eat_more.food: Fluids — water, coconut water, fresh fruit juice
eat_more.reason: Fever causes rapid dehydration. Drink at least 8-10 glasses daily during illness.
If not keeping fluids down well, ORS replaces salts lost in fever and vomiting
Iron to rebuild blood destroyed by malaria. Also B vitamins for recovery.
Vitamin A strengthens immunity and helps recovery. Malaria depletes Vitamin A.
Appetite is poor during malaria. Small amounts frequently is better than forcing large meals.
Zinc is depleted during infection and is essential for immune recovery
Iron, Vitamin C, and multiple micronutrients — excellent recovery food
Vitamin C with every iron-rich meal doubles iron absorption for anaemia recovery

eat_less.food: Tea and coffee during recovery (large amounts)
eat_less.reason: Reduces iron absorption when trying to rebuild blood

eat_less.food: Fatty fried foods in acute illness
eat_less.reason: Hard to digest when liver is under strain from malaria
Suppress immune function

plans.special_note: Take the complete course of anti-malarial medication (all 6 doses of artemether-lumefantrine) regardless of how you feel. Nutrition cannot replace medication. Children recovering from malaria should also receive a Vitamin A capsule if not had one in 3 months.
plans.uganda_note: Malaria is the most common cause of anaemia in Uganda's children. A child with repeated malaria becomes progressively more anaemic. Iron supplementation alongside malaria treatment is recommended. Insecticide-treated nets prevent malaria — use them every night.

plans.name: The Uganda Healthy Plate (General Nutrition)
plans.intro: Uganda has exceptional nutritional diversity — a wide variety of traditional foods that together form a complete, affordable, and healthy diet. The challenge is not lack of food variety but ensuring balance and variety in daily meals.
plans.goal: A balanced, varied diet using affordable Ugandan foods for overall health

half_plate.tip: The more colours, the more nutrients

quarter_plate.tip: Millet and sorghum are healthier than refined white posho and white rice

superfoods_uganda.name: Moringa (Muwungu)
superfoods_uganda.why: Contains iron, calcium, Vitamin A, C, protein — exceptional nutrition. Powder from dried leaves can be added to any food.

superfoods_uganda.name: Orange Sweet Potato (OFSP)
superfoods_uganda.why: Rich in beta-carotene (Vitamin A) — critical for child eye health and immunity. Uganda promotes OFSP nationally.

superfoods_uganda.name: Mukene (Silver cyprinid fish)
superfoods_uganda.why: Whole small fish — eaten with bones, providing calcium, iron, B12, and protein. Most affordable complete protein.

superfoods_uganda.name: Simsim (Sesame)
superfoods_uganda.why: Calcium, iron, and healthy fats. Ground into paste (simsim paste / tahini) is one of Africa's most nutritious traditional foods.

superfoods_uganda.name: Termites (Ngwen/Enswa — white ants)
superfoods_uganda.why: Seasonal (November-December). Exceptionally high in protein, zinc, iron, and healthy fats. Traditional Ugandan superfood.

superfoods_uganda.name: Avocado (Ovakado)
superfoods_uganda.why: Healthy fats, potassium, folate, Vitamin E. Available year-round in Uganda and relatively affordable.

superfoods_uganda.name: Beans (all types)
superfoods_uganda.why: Iron, protein, fibre, B vitamins. The backbone of a healthy affordable Ugandan diet.

plans.water_guidance: Drink at least 6-8 glasses (1.5-2 litres) of clean water daily. Boil or treat water from unsafe sources. Breastfeeding mothers need 3+ litres daily. Sodas, Fanta, juice drinks are not water.
plans.uganda_warning: Key nutritional gaps in many Ugandan diets: (1) Not enough Vitamin A — eat orange sweet potato, pumpkin, mango, eggs, liver. (2) Insufficient iron — eat beans with lemon/tomato, liver, moringa. (3) Too much salt from Royco/Maggi cubes and salted dried fish. (4) Too many refined carbohydrates replacing traditional millet/sorghum.

plans.name: Nutrition During Pregnancy
plans.intro: A mother's diet during pregnancy directly shapes her baby's development, birth weight, brain growth, and lifelong health. In Uganda, where malnutrition and anaemia in pregnant women are common, getting nutrition right is critical.
plans.goal: Support mother's health and baby's growth while preventing anaemia and deficiency

eat_more.reason: Blood volume increases 50% in pregnancy — massive iron demand
eat_more.tip: Always with Vitamin C food to double absorption

eat_more.reason: Prevents neural tube defects (spina bifida) — CRITICAL in first trimester
eat_more.supplement: Also take folic acid 400mcg tablet daily (or 5mg if on cotrimoxazole)

eat_more.reason: Baby's bone formation + prevents pre-eclampsia
eat_more.supplement: Calcium 1.5g/day supplement recommended from 20 weeks in Uganda (reduces pre-eclampsia risk 50%)

eat_more.reason: Baby's organ and brain development
Vitamin A for baby's immune system and vision
eat_more.caution: Avoid high-dose Vitamin A supplements (above 10,000 IU) — teratogenic in excess

eat_more.reason: Amniotic fluid, increased blood volume, kidney function

eat_less.reason: Risk of Toxoplasma, Salmonella, Listeria — all dangerous in pregnancy
Teratogenic at high doses — food sources are safe
Fetal alcohol syndrome — no safe amount in pregnancy
Salmonella risk
Brucellosis risk (especially in cattle-keeping areas)

antenatal_supplements: Folic acid 400mcg daily (5mg if on cotrimoxazole)
Vitamin A in postpartum period (NOT high doses in pregnancy)
plans.antenatal_care: Attend all antenatal visits. Target: at least 4 visits in pregnancy. Blood pressure checked at every visit detects pre-eclampsia early. Iron and folic acid given free at government antenatal clinics.
plans.uganda_note: Anaemia affects over 40% of Ugandan pregnant women and is a major cause of maternal death (by increasing risk of haemorrhage). Every pregnant Ugandan woman should receive and take iron-folic acid tablets throughout pregnancy. Orange-fleshed sweet potato has been promoted nationally for its Vitamin A content — highly recommended in pregnancy.

foods_database.name: Beans (Obwobe/Ebijanjaalo)
foods_database.notes: Uganda's most affordable everyday protein and iron. Always pair with Vitamin C food for best iron absorption. Cook from scratch — tinned beans less available and more expensive.

foods_database.name: Liver (Chicken/Goat — Lifu/Enkoko)
foods_database.notes: Most concentrated iron and B12 source available in Uganda. 100g liver twice weekly dramatically improves anaemia. Eat in moderation in pregnancy (avoid exceeding 1-2 portions/week due to high Vitamin A).

foods_database.name: Moringa leaves (Muwungu)
foods_database.notes: Uganda's nutritional superfood — rare combination of iron AND Vitamin C in same food. Dried powder can be added to any food. Grows easily in backyard. Fresh leaves in soups and stews.

foods_database.name: Mukene (Silver Cyprinid fish — Dagaa)
foods_database.notes: Eaten whole — bones provide calcium. Most affordable complete protein source in Uganda. Very high calcium when bones eaten. Lake Victoria and Lake Albert supply. Buy and store dried — long shelf life.

foods_database.name: Orange Sweet Potato (OFSP)
foods_database.notes: Uganda promotes orange sweet potato nationally for Vitamin A. One medium OFSP provides entire daily Vitamin A need. Far healthier than ordinary white-fleshed sweet potato. Can identify by bright orange flesh.

foods_database.name: Sukuma Wiki (Kale)
foods_database.notes: Name means 'stretch the week' in Swahili — extremely affordable nutrition. Cook briefly (do not overcook) to preserve vitamins. Available year-round across Uganda.

foods_database.name: Groundnuts (Ebinyeebwa)
foods_database.notes: Essential protein and fat source in Ugandan diet. Groundnut stew (peanut sauce) is nutritious when not overly salted. Grind into paste for spreading. Avoid mouldy groundnuts — aflatoxin risk.

foods_database.name: Simsim (Sesame)
foods_database.notes: Extremely high in iron AND calcium — one of few plant foods with both. Grind into paste for spreading. Toast and sprinkle on foods. Common in northern Uganda and available nationally.

foods_database.name: Avocado (Ovakado)
foods_database.notes: Excellent source of potassium (better than banana per serving). Healthy fat helps absorption of fat-soluble vitamins from other foods. Available cheaply across Uganda in season.

foods_database.name: Guava (Pera)
foods_database.notes: Uganda's highest Vitamin C fruit — far higher than orange. Affordable and widely available. Eat the pink-fleshed varieties for highest lycopene too. Vitamin C dramatically improves iron absorption from plant sources.

foods_database.name: Amaranth / Dodo
foods_database.notes: Traditional Ugandan leafy vegetable, often overlooked for modern vegetables. Highly nutritious and drought-tolerant — grows easily. Seeds also nutritious. Prepare like sukuma wiki.

foods_database.name: Millet (Obulo / Finger Millet)
foods_database.notes: Traditional Ugandan grain with far superior nutrition to refined white posho. Calcium content exceptional for a grain. Low glycaemic index — ideal for diabetics. Fermented millet porridge (obushera) is excellent for children. Being replaced by white posho — important to preserve use.

foods_database.name: Sorghum (Emwenge / Odunga)
foods_database.notes: Traditional Ugandan grain — nutritionally superior to maize posho. Drought-tolerant — important food security crop in northern Uganda. Can be used for porridge, ugali, and brewing. Low GI — good for diabetics.

foods_database.name: Banana / Matoke (Empogola/Gonja)
foods_database.notes: Uganda's national staple. Matoke (cooking banana) is the foundation of many Ugandan meals. High potassium helpful for blood pressure. Ripe bananas raise blood sugar faster than unripe — diabetics should use green/unripe matoke. Gonja (plantain) is good for fibre.

foods_database.name: Pumpkin (Omuzigo/Enseke)
foods_database.notes: Very affordable and widely available across Uganda. Both flesh and seeds nutritious. Seeds: high iron and zinc. Pumpkin leaves also edible and nutritious. Excellent Vitamin A source for children.

foods_database.name: Eggs (Amagi)
foods_database.notes: One of the most complete nutritious foods available. The egg yolk contains most of the nutrition — do not discard it. Affordable source of complete protein and Vitamin B12. Daily egg for children, pregnant women, and anyone with anaemia is excellent.

foods_database.name: Tilapia / Nile Perch (Emputa/Ngege)
foods_database.notes: Uganda's most widely eaten freshwater fish from lakes Victoria, Albert, George. Excellent lean protein. Lake Victoria Nile perch widely exported — tilapia more commonly eaten locally. Affordable near lakeshores.

foods_database.name: Termites (Ngwen / Enswa — white ants)
foods_database.notes: Seasonal Ugandan delicacy (November-December) — nutritionally exceptional. Higher iron than beef, higher protein than many meats. Traditional food eaten fried or dried. Nutritionally underappreciated. Harvested sustainably.

foods_database.name: Coconut (Njigo)
foods_database.notes: More common in coastal / eastern Uganda. Coconut water is an excellent oral rehydration fluid. Coconut oil for cooking and skin. Use in moderation — very calorie dense.

foods_database.name: Cassava (Muwogo)
foods_database.notes: Major staple especially in northern Uganda. Nutritionally, primarily an energy (starch) food — very low in protein, iron, and vitamins. MUST be paired with protein (beans, fish, groundnuts) and vegetables at every meal to prevent malnutrition. Fermented cassava and cassava leaves have more nutritional value. Do not rely on cassava alone.

foods_database.name: Mango (Emyembe)
foods_database.notes: Abundant seasonal fruit in Uganda (main season: Oct-Jan, with shorter rains season). Very high Vitamin A and C when ripe. Cheap and widely available in season. Eat with meals to enhance iron absorption from beans and vegetables.
